results.title: A machine learning system to optimise triage in an adult ophthalmic ...
results.content: ### Interpretation At MEH, DOTS had similar sensitivity to triage nurses in determining attendance priority; however, with a specificity of 17.3% higher, DOTS resulted in lower rates of patients triaged to be seen immediately at emergency. ### Implications of all the available evidence The developed system had similar sensitivity to triage nurses in determining attendance priority (∼ 95%); however, with a specificity up to 17.3% higher, the model resulted in lower rates of patients triaged to be seen immediately at emergency. Ophthalmology is the busiest speciality by outpatient workload in the United Kingdom (UK) and demand for eye care has outgrown the workforce worldwide.1,2 New attendances in emergency departments have been on the rise, accounting for over 30% of all ophthalmic attendances in National Health Service (NHS) England.3,4 Notably, the proportion of patients presenting with non-urgent conditions is significant (>15%) yet providing non-urgent care can be three times more costly than similar attendances in other settings.5,6 Machine learning (ML) is being increasingly applied to improve clinical workflow efficiency and has the potential to enhance the accuracy of triage, optimising service allocation.7 Within triage, ML has the capability to process high dimensionality structured data and the potential to achieve superior performance compared to rule-based algorithms by abstracting complex non-linear patterns between patients’ clinical presentation and their clinical risk. Our tabular dataset used to build DOTS consists of presentations to Europe’s largest eye emergency department over a 1-year period encompassing anterior and posterior segment pathologies.3 We conducted bias analyses in demographic subgroups within TVal and EVal. Our demographic data reflects the difficulty of collecting patient ethnicity in healthcare settings, with more than 58% of attendances in TVal being registered in the system as of “other” or “unknown” ethnicities. In this study, we developed and validated DOTS, an ML-based system to support triage nurses in ophthalmic emergency, using data from over 13,000 emergency attendances. In temporal validation, DOTS presented equivalent sensitivity to triage nurses to determine attendance priority, but a specificity 17.3% higher, so identifying 10.5% fewer patients, who did not need to be seen immediately at emergency. In external validation, DOTS presented equivalent sensitivity to triage nurses at MEH to determine attendance priority and was 7.1% more specific to emergencies.

results.title: Mortality predictors in pediatric emergency department presentations: a systematic review and meta-analysis | BMC Emergency Medicine | Full Text
results.content: 329 Pediatric Early Warning Score (PEWS) thresholds were analyzed, with the model-derived optimal cutoff 2.189 (AUC) = 0.70; 95% CI: 0.63 to 0.76), high pooled sensitivity (0.95, 95% CI: 0.72 to 0.80) and specificity (0.93, 95% CI: 0.62 to 0.80). Scoring systems such as the Pediatric Early Warning Score (PEWS), Pediatric Risk of Mortality (PRISM), and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) have been developed to help identify pediatric patients at risk of mortality, increasing monitoring and escalation with the appropriate emergency and critical care skills [2:e014497.")]. Our systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate mortality predictors (e.g., PEWS, PRISM, SOFA) in PEDs, focusing on the predictive accuracy of clinical variables and scoring systems, including sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic odds ratio. To evaluate the diagnostic performance of PEWS in predicting mortality, we conducted random-effects meta-analyses of sensitivity and specificity using data pooled across multiple studies. The pooled diagnostic accuracy of the Pediatric Early Warning Score (PEWS) revealed high estimates for both sensitivity and specificity (Figs. These findings affirm that PEWS consistently identifies at-risk patients across diverse settings, supporting its utility as a sensitivity-optimized early detection tool in pediatric emergency care. These findings suggest a low risk of small-study effects or selective reporting, reinforcing the robustness of pooled NPV estimates and supporting their clinical validity as rule-out tools in pediatric mortality prediction. * **Cardiac Children’s Hospital Early Warning Score (C-CHEWS)**: Reported sensitivity values as high as 0.98 and strong NPV suggest that C-CHEWS may serve as a robust early detection tool for clinical deterioration in pediatric patients. Overall, the pooled analyses affirm that early warning scores demonstrate high negative predictive value and modest diagnostic discrimination for pediatric mortality. This aligns with previous studies on early warning scores (EWS) in adult populations, where high sensitivity and low specificity are common [43,44:119–26."),45 in predicting serious adverse events among patients presenting to emergency departments of Muhimbili National Hospital and MUHAS Academic Medical Center. While the high pooled NPV underscores PEWS’ value in excluding imminent mortality risk, it is important to acknowledge that this metric is heavily influenced by the low prevalence of pediatric mortality in most emergency settings.
